主要内容: On July 10, 2013, the SEC adopted bad actor disqualification provisions for Rule 506 of Regulation D under the Securities Act of 1933, to implement Section 926 of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. These provisions, appearing as paragraphs (d) and (e) of Rule 506 of Regulation D, disqualify offerings from relying on Rule 506(b) and 506(c) if the issuer or any other person covered by Rule 506(d) has a relevant criminal conviction, regulatory or court order, or other disqualifying event that occurred on or after September 23, 2013, the effective date of the rule amendments. Under Rule 506(e), issuers may still rely on Rule 506 for disqualifying events that occurred before September 23, 2013, but must comply with the disclosure provisions of Rule 506(e). The SEC has finalized rules that disqualify certain individuals, including felons and other 'bad actors,' from participating in Rule 506 offerings. These rules also outline disclosure requirements for such offerings. Key categories of disqualified individuals include beneficial owners holding 20% or more of the issuer’s equity securities, promoters, investment managers, and compensated solicitors. Disqualifying events include criminal convictions, court injunctions, regulatory orders, and SEC cease-and-desist orders. The look-back period for these events is measured from the date of the disqualifying event, not the date of the underlying conduct. For example, a criminal conviction related to false filings must occur within ten years of the proposed sale of securities, or five years in the case of the issuer and its predecessors. These rules aim to enhance investor protection and ensure compliance with securities regulations. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) issued guidance on September 19, 2013, regarding the disqualification of individuals with criminal convictions or other 'bad actor' status from Rule 506 offerings. Under the updated rules, issuers must disclose any disqualifying events in writing to investors before a Rule 506 sale. The disclosure is required regardless of when the underlying conduct occurred, as long as the triggering event (such as a criminal conviction or regulatory order) occurs after the rule amendments took effect on September 23, 2013. The SEC emphasized that the form of disclosure should be prominent to ensure investors are adequately informed. Sales made before the effective date of the amendments are not subject to these disqualification and disclosure requirements, even if they are part of an ongoing offering. Disqualifying events that occur during an offering may affect subsequent sales, unless the issuer can demonstrate it was unaware of the event and exercised reasonable care. The guidance is a compliance tool under the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 and is not a substitute for the actual rules.
